common_name: Twilight Magic Crapemyrtle (Plum-Foliage Disease-Resistant Purple-Leaf Alternative)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Twilight Magic is a First Editions crapemyrtle bred for deep plum foliage with high resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew, marketed as a heat-tolerant, disease-resistant alternative to purple-leaf plum trees that often defoliate in Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Twilight Magic bears deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color through the heat of a Gulf South summer, providing dramatic contrast against clusters of fuchsia-pink blooms from summer into fall. It was bred with high resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew, holding its dark foliage cleanly through humid conditions that cause many purple-leaved landscape shrubs and small trees to decline or defoliate. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural form rather than heavily topping it.
sources: First Editions — US Plant Patent PP27,194

common_name: Berry Dazzle Crapemyrtle (Dwarf Mildew-Resistant Fuchsia-Pink Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Berry Dazzle is a true dwarf crapemyrtle, staying about 4 feet tall, bred with powdery mildew resistance and fuchsia-pink blooms, well suited to a small Gulf Coast bed or container.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Berry Dazzle is a genuine dwarf crapemyrtle, staying about 4 feet tall and wide, bred with resistance to powdery mildew so its foliage stays clean through the humidity of a Gulf South summer while producing a heavy show of fuchsia-pink blooms. Its compact size makes it well suited to small foundation plantings, mixed borders, or large containers where a tree-form crapemyrtle would be far too large. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through summer and fall. Because of its naturally compact habit, Berry Dazzle needs little pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood in late winter.

common_name: Gatsby Gal Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact White-to-Pink Blooming Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Gal is a Proven Winners selection in the Gatsby series of oakleaf hydrangeas, chosen for a compact, well-proportioned habit that fits more easily into a residential landscape than the full-sized species.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gatsby Gal produces large, elongated flower panicles that open white in early summer and take on a soft pink blush as they age, on a more compact plant than the straight oakleaf hydrangea species, making it easier to fit into a foundation planting or shade border. Like all oakleaf hydrangeas, it is a Southeastern US native fully adapted to the heat, humidity, and clay soils of the Gulf South, developing excellent burgundy-red fall foliage and attractive peeling bark for winter interest. Requires little pruning; remove only dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth by late summer.

common_name: Gatsby Pink Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large White-to-Deep-Pink Color-Shift Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Pink is a Proven Winners oakleaf hydrangea noted for an especially dramatic color transformation, with large white blooms deepening to rich pink through the summer.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Gatsby Pink produces large, showy flower panicles that open pure white in early summer and gradually deepen to a rich, saturated pink as they age through the season, giving an extended, ever-changing floral display. Its full-sized habit fits well in a woodland border or mass planting where its bold texture and multi-season interest can be appreciated. Like other oakleaf hydrangeas, it develops burgundy-red fall foliage and attractive cinnamon, peeling bark for winter interest, and is fully adapted to the heat, humidity, and clay soils of the Gulf South. Requires little pruning; remove only dead or crossing wood right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth.

common_name: Scarlet Beauty Virginia Sweetspire (Heat-Tolerant Morton Arboretum Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Scarlet Beauty was selected at the Morton Arboretum for superior heat and soil pH tolerance compared with other Itea cultivars, along with an especially fiery multi-colored fall display.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Scarlet Beauty was selected at the Morton Arboretum for producing fragrant, drooping, bottlebrush-like white flower clusters in early summer followed by an especially vivid fall display that blends red, orange, and yellow, often several colors on a single leaf, and for tolerating a wider range of soil pH and heat than many other named Itea selections. Like other sweetspire cultivars it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil better than most landscape shrubs, making it an excellent choice for a rain garden or low-lying moist spot in the Gulf South landscape. It spreads gradually by suckering to form a colony over time, useful for naturalizing or streambank stabilization. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood; it develops excellent fall color even in partial shade.
